content.text:
Nature and science facts about cats

Cats were domesticated from wild cats about 9,500 years ago. Thanks to a reflective layer at the back of their eyes, they can see with six times less light than a human, and they sense the width of their body and vibrations in the air through their whiskers. With their rough tongues they spend 30–50% of their waking hours grooming, and they can twist their bodies and land on their feet in half a second. A cat's purr signals not only happiness but also anxiety or pain.

Parent guide — how to spark curiosity

Observe a cat's whiskers without touching them, and talk about the roughness of its tongue (grooming). Guessing the cat's mood together when it purrs nurtures a caring heart toward animals.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why can cats see well even in the dark?
A. Thanks to a reflective layer at the back of their eyes, they can see with six times less light than a human.

Q. What do a cat's whiskers do?
A. They are a sensory organ that gauges the width of the body and detects vibrations in the air. You shouldn't touch them carelessly.

Q. How can we observe them at home?
A. Observe the whiskers without touching them, and guess the cat's mood from its grooming and purring.
